p.title: Contingency-Aware Influence Maximization: A Reinforcement Learning Approach

ext.title: Contingency-Aware Influence Maximization: A Reinforcement Learning Approach
ext.venue: Accepted to UAI 2021 (37th Conference on Uncertainty in Artificial Intelligence); arXiv:2106.07039v1 [cs.SI], 13 Jun 2021. The metadata hint said "arXiv preprint (v1)"; the PDF states UAI 2021 acceptance, so the venue is corrected.
ext.document_type: Conference paper (UAI 2021), arXiv preprint v1; algorithm paper with simulation experiments
ext.coverage: Full text read in chunks (all 1341 extracted lines: front matter, abstract, introduction, related work, problem setup, MDP formulation, RL4IM algorithm, state abstraction, reward shaping and theorems, experiments, conclusion, references). Paul's annotation file was read in full: 35 highlight items on pages 1-4, none with note text. Figures 1-5 are covered through captions and axis labels only, since plotted values are not in the extracted text. Lobbying, elections, persuasion/turnout, legislators, text measurement and path-finding are absent from the paper. Network content is seed selection for influence spread. Allocation appears only as a per-round budget of B seeds over T rounds, not economic allocation. Highlight colors vary (yellow, green, blue, pink) and the file has no legend.
ext.research_question: How to choose seed nodes for influence maximization when each invited node is only probabilistically willing to accept (contingency-aware IM), at low computational cost on new social networks, using reinforcement learning that generalizes to unseen networks without re-running an expensive greedy algorithm (Abstract p.1; Introduction p.1-2).
ext.theory: Influence spreads under the Independent Cascade (IC) model (Goldenberg et al. 2001; Kempe et al. 2003), Sec 3.1 p.3. Seed willingness is Bernoulli with a known probability q, Sec 3.1 p.3. The influence function is treated as submodular (stated as "usually submodular", Sec 4.3 p.4). The sequential decision is a discrete-time MDP with sub-steps (t,b), Sec 3.2 p.3-4. The learner is DQN with structure2vec-style graph embeddings (Khalil et al. 2017), Sec 4.1 p.4. The key derived result is a surrogate reward (Eq. 11, Theorem 1, p.4) under assumptions Eqs. 9-10 (marginal contribution depends only on the count of willing predecessors; arithmetic-sequence form).
ext.data: Synthetic graphs only. Power-law graphs from a Barabasi-Albert growth model with an extra triangle step (Onnela et al. 2007): average degree 3, triangle probability 0.05, Sec 5.1 p.5. Unit of observation: graph and seed node. Default |V|=200 nodes, T=2 rounds, B=4 per round (budget 8), q=0.6, 200 training graphs, 5 validation graphs, 10 unseen test graphs, each run 20 times (200 runs per setting), Sec 5.1-5.2 p.5-6. Influence propagation probability 0.1 in experiments (text reads "belief propagation probability", Sec 5.1 p.5). One real-scale runtime reference: CHANGE on a 1000-node, 4974-edge network, propagation probability 0.2, sampling frequency 50, one Intel i9-9820X core; runtime reaches about 10 hours at 20 seeds (Figure 1, p.1-2). Experiment hardware: 2 Xeon Gold 6148 cores, 5 GB RAM, one Tesla V100 (Sec 5.1 p.5). Time period: not stated. No human sample or N of people. The HIV-prevention, homeless-youth setting (Yadav et al. 2016, 2018; Wilder et al. 2018) is the motivating application only.
ext.method: Reinforcement learning for influence maximization (RL4IM), Sec 4, p.4-5. (1) Each sub-step selects one node; the state is a 3 x |V| binary matrix (unselected; selected-willing; selected-unwilling; selected-unknown) plus fixed graph G, Sec 3.2 p.3-4. (2) State abstraction: X_bar = X1 + q*X3 (Eq. 5, Sec 4.2 p.4), with a feasible-action set maintained separately for unwilling nodes. (3) Reward shaping: the exact expected marginal reward (Eq. 6) is replaced by r~ = (1-q)*dI0 + q*dI_{b-1} (Eq. 11, Theorem 1), where dI0 and dI_{b-1} bound the marginal contribution (Lemma 1, Eq. 8). Theorem 2: reward computation falls from O(2^b) to O(1). Theorem 3 gives the gap bound max{(q-(1-q)^{b-1})(dI0-dI_{b-1}), (1-q-q^{b-1})(dI0-dI_{b-1})}. (4) Training: DQN with experience replay (memory 4096, batch 32, max 2000 training steps, discount 0.99, S2V embedding + 128-unit MLP, Adam), Sec 5.1 p.5. Baselines: CHANGE greedy (Wilder et al. 2018), S2V-DQN-IM (state abstraction added; reward uses dI_{b-1}), and Random. Validation uses 20 episodes x 5 graphs per checkpoint; IM spread is simulated 100 times per estimate.
ext.identification: None in the causal sense. This is an algorithm and simulation study with no quasi-experimental or observational identification. Performance is measured on held-out synthetic graphs: validation graphs select hyperparameters and checkpoints, and unseen test graphs measure generalization. Theorem 3 bounds the approximation gap of the surrogate reward under Eqs. 9-10, which are stated assumptions, not identified facts.
ext.scope: Population: synthetic power-law social networks, with a real-scale runtime illustration only (Figure 1). Institutions: Harvard Center for Research on Computation and Society; Nanyang Technological University (p.1). Era: arXiv June 2021, UAI 2021. Application framing: low-resource non-profits running HIV-prevention peer-leader interventions among homeless youth (Introduction p.1-2; Section 3 p.3). Generalization is claimed only across synthetic graphs with similar characteristics (Introduction p.2).

key_findings.finding: Formulates contingency-aware IM as a discrete-time MDP in which each sub-step selects one node; the state is the willingness matrix plus the fixed graph. The time horizon is T x B.
key_findings.numbers: T x B sub-steps; state X in {0,1}^(3 x |V|)

key_findings.finding: Surrogate reward (Eq. 11) replaces the exact expected marginal contribution with (1-q)*dI0 + q*dI_{b-1}, under assumptions Eqs. 9-10.
The surrogate cuts reward computation from O(2^b) to O(1) per sub-step, using 4 influence evaluations.
key_findings.numbers: O(2^b) reduced to O(1); 4 influence values

key_findings.finding: The gap between surrogate and exact reward is bounded, but the bound can be arbitrarily bad as q approaches 0 or 1. Authors say these cases are rare and that RL4IM still works at q=0.2 and q=0.8.
Ablation Q1: removing state abstraction or reward shaping makes training unstable or converges to a sub-optimal point. Figure 3 shows validation curves; numeric values are not in the extracted text.
Q2: more training graphs give a more stable validation curve. The paper uses 200 training graphs for all later experiments.
Q3: across q, RL4IM and CHANGE both reach roughly twice Random and are more stable; S2V-DQN-IM is unstable. Expected influence rises with q.
key_findings.numbers: roughly 2x Random; figure axis labels -0.05 to 0.2; plotted values not in text

key_findings.finding: Q4: with T x B fixed at 8, RL4IM works for single-round IM (T=1); CHANGE and RL4IM are the two best methods.
Q5: normalized influence falls as graph size grows from 50 to 1000 nodes with budget fixed at 8; CHANGE and RL4IM are best.

Overall, RL4IM matches or slightly exceeds CHANGE. Authors attribute the edge to proactively modeling unwillingness in the reward, versus CHANGE reacting to realized willingness. Authors claim near-zero test runtime (policy in seconds on a laptop).
key_findings.location: Sec 5.2 p.6 (paragraph after Q5); Conclusion p.6
key_findings.numbers: 'slightly better than CHANGE'; runtime 'within seconds' (no measured figure given)

key_findings.finding: Runtime motivation: CHANGE needs about 10 hours even with 20 seeds on a 1000-node, 4974-edge network.

limitations: The surrogate reward rests on assumptions (Eqs. 9-10: marginal contribution depends only on the count of willing nodes; arithmetic-sequence form) and on submodularity of influence (Eq. 7; stated as 'usually submodular', p.4). The paper does not test these on real data.
The Theorem 3 gap bound can be arbitrarily bad as q goes to 0 or 1; the authors call these cases rare and extreme (p.5).
Willingness probability q is assumed known a priori and identical across nodes (footnote 2, p.3; Sec 3.1 p.3).
Experiments use synthetic power-law graphs only, with IC propagation probability 0.1 (p.5). The only real-scale measurement is the CHANGE runtime in Figure 1.
Only the IC model is evaluated.
No training cost (wall-clock or GPU hours) is reported. The 'negligible runtime at test phase' claim is qualitative ('within seconds', p.6).
Baselines are one greedy algorithm (CHANGE) and one RL baseline (S2V-DQN-IM with state abstraction added). Other contingency-aware methods, such as the Yadav et al. POMDP, are not benchmarked.
Key figure results (Figures 3-5) are described only qualitatively in the text; plotted values are not stated numerically.
The single-round setting (T=1) is evaluated only on synthetic graphs (p.6).
measures: Expected normalized influence: spread divided by |V|, averaged over 200 runs per setting (Figure 5 caption, p.6).
Validation metric: average reward over 20 episodes x 5 validation graphs = 100 runs, used to choose hyperparameters and checkpoints (Sec 5.1 p.5).
Runtime of CHANGE versus seed count (Figure 1, p.1-2; reported in hours).
Validation curves of expected influence versus training steps (Figures 3-4).

rel.summary_md:
Chen, Qiu, Ou, An and Tambe (UAI 2021) study contingency-aware influence maximization. In this setting an invited seed accepts only with a probability q, which is known in advance and the same for every node. Seeds are chosen over T rounds of B seeds, and willingness is revealed only at the end of each round. The authors cast the problem as an MDP and train a DQN with structure2vec embeddings (RL4IM). Two devices make training tractable: a state abstraction (X1 + q*X3) and a surrogate reward, (1-q)*dI0 + q*dI_{b-1}. The surrogate cuts reward computation from O(2^b) to O(1), and Theorem 3 bounds its gap from the exact reward, though the bound becomes arbitrarily loose as q approaches 0 or 1. All experiments use synthetic Barabasi-Albert-type graphs: 200 nodes, Independent Cascade with p=0.1, q=0.6, budget 8, and 200 runs per setting. On these graphs RL4IM matches or slightly beats the CHANGE greedy baseline, and both reach roughly twice Random. The paper's case for RL is runtime on new, unseen networks: CHANGE takes about 10 hours at 20 seeds on a 1,000-node graph. It gives no empirical estimate of q for any real population.

For Melange the paper is the cited source of the SGATE contingency gate (fec/moneyball_core.py:626-630). The gate is used non-adaptively in the coalition and frontier spread estimators. The system goes beyond the paper's model in three ways: q varies by member (seed_prob x stance gate), there is a single round with no observed willingness, and committed allies are never gated. The paper's theorems do not cover that model, and the system does not need them, because it estimates expected spread directly by Monte Carlo. The paper does not validate any take-up rate. The 0.60 baseline in seed_prob equals the paper's arbitrary simulation default. The planned H1 test correlates seed_prob with unconditional new cosponsorships, which is not the conditional-on-invitation quantity the paper models. The runtime argument for RL does not apply to a fixed 533-member chamber graph. All agent analysis here is UNVERIFIED (DE-062).

bearings.paper_claim: Contingency-aware IM: a selected seed is willing only with a Bernoulli probability q, which is known a priori and identical across nodes (Sec 3.1, footnote 2). Experiments use q=0.6 by default and test q=0.2 and 0.8. No real-world value of q is estimated.
bearings.paper_location: Sec 3.1 p.3 (footnote 2); Sec 5.1 p.5; Q3 Fig 5(a) p.6
bearings.system_side: gate(n) = max(0.15, seed_prob(n) x SGATE[tier]). SGATE runs from Highly Persuadable 1.00 down to Opponent 0.35, with unknown at 0.85. The effective take-up prior therefore spans 0.15 to 0.90 and differs by member. Ally, Champion and Defender are set to 1.0, and in the spread estimators the pro core is unconditional rather than gated. seed_prob = clip(0.60 + .10 coop + .06 breadth + .04 visibility, 0.30, 0.90). Its 0.60 baseline equals the paper's simulation default q, which was chosen for the simulation and is not an estimate.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Only the modeling idea transfers: invitation is not activation. The paper's q is homogeneous and its analysis is multi-round. SGATE is heterogeneous, graded by stance and personality, and used single-shot, so Theorems 1-3 do not cover it. The paper gives no evidence for any SGATE level or for the 0.60 baseline. The source population is HIV peer leaders among homeless youth, not legislators. Until H1 or a contact log measures take-up, SGATE values remain owner design priors.

bearings.paper_claim: Modeling unwillingness inside the objective, rather than reacting to realized willingness, is the authors' explanation for RL4IM matching or slightly beating greedy CHANGE. At T=1 (single round, T x B = 8) RL4IM and CHANGE remain the two best methods, and both reach roughly twice Random. All results come from synthetic power-law graphs under IC with p=0.1.
bearings.paper_location: Q3-Q4, Sec 5.2 p.6; paragraph after Q5 p.6; Fig 5(a)-(b)
bearings.system_side: Lazy greedy up to 60 seeds. spread() draws each lobbied seed's activation against gate(n,cs) on a dedicated CRN stream at key offset 2^62 (lines 126-128), so the expectation over willingness sits inside the greedy objective. A failed contest activation leaves the target an opponent (lines 129-131). This is non-adaptive single-round contingency-aware IM on an IC-type competitive cascade.
bearings.transfer_conditions: This supports the design choice of putting take-up uncertainty into the expected-spread objective. It does not validate the cascade kernel, the gate values or the two-colour competition; the paper models a single colour only. The evidence is synthetic graphs at about 200 nodes, which is comparable in scale to the 533-member graph, but there are no political data. The 'slightly better' edge is reported qualitatively, with no numbers.

bearings.paper_claim: Under contingency, the exact expected marginal contribution of a seed depends on which earlier seeds turned out willing (O(2^b) cases). Influence is assumed submodular (Eq. 7).
bearings.system_side: The coalition allocator computes each candidate's individual marginal spread({n}) - base with the seed gate inside the MC loop. It then water-fills the budget on those individual marginals and reports the honest joint spread of the funded set, because summing individual marginals overstates the joint gain (M2 fix).
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper's O(2^b) dependence on earlier seeds' willingness is the same non-additivity that the joint-spread report exposes. Allocating on single-seed marginals ignores that dependence. The paper's surrogate reward is one cheap correction, but it needs a homogeneous q and its Eqs. 9-10 assumptions, so it would not port directly to heterogeneous gates. This is a diagnostic allocator, so the stakes are low.

bearings.paper_claim: q is the probability that a node is willing when it is selected or invited. It is a conditional take-up rate that the paper assumes known a priori.
bearings.system_side: H1 ('seeding, Chen/SNAM') tests Spearman(frozen seed_prob, NEW cosponsorships after the freeze) over all covered members. Engaged-only scoring is unavailable until receipted contact data exists. The F5 replay found 72 of 511 new-event members against a 150-member floor, so H1 is UNDERPOWERED and its look is unspent.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Unconditional new cosponsorship mixes the take-up rate with who gets contacted and with base activity. Chen's q is defined conditional on an invitation. A pass on unconditional H1 would therefore not validate seed_prob as a contingency probability, and a miss would not refute it. The construct match needs the engaged-only arm, that is, a contact log.

gaps_exposed: The system never observes or updates willingness. The paper's setting is multi-round: willingness is revealed at the end of each round and later seeds are chosen knowing it. Melange seeding is a one-shot plan. Replanning after observed take-up would need an outreach or contact log, which does not exist.
No empirical take-up rate backs either SGATE or seed_prob. The paper supplies none for any population, and the 0.60 baseline equals its arbitrary simulation default.
The H1 receptivity contract measures unconditional cosponsorship, not take-up conditional on contact. The construct Chen defines cannot be tested until receipted contact data exists.

The paper shows that a seed's marginal value depends on earlier seeds' realized willingness. The coalition allocator funds on individual gated marginals and only reports the joint shortfall afterwards. It does not fund on conditional marginals.
flags: Language: seed_prob x SGATE is a heuristic design prior. Do not describe it as a measured take-up, access or commitment probability for a legislator. The paper validates no q for any real population, and H1 is unspent and underpowered (72/511 against a 150 floor).

Paul's addendum files Chen 2021 under 'C. RL influence maximization - the non-submodular envelope'. The paper explicitly assumes submodularity (Eq. 7) and IC. The non-submodular, complex-contagion work is the same group's RL4CCIM (chen-nd-complex-contagion-influence). Chen 2021 should not be cited as evidence for the non-submodular tier.

Paul's takeaway describes the method as 'observe-then-act'. That is accurate only between rounds; within a round willingness is unknown and is replaced by its expectation (X1 + q*X3). The system as built observes nothing (single-shot), so the 'observe-then-act' framing describes an unbuilt capability.

The paper's motivation for RL (repeated recomputation on new graphs by low-compute NGOs) does not apply to Melange's fixed 533-member chamber graphs. Its quality result is parity with greedy. Neither supports replacing the CELF or lazy-greedy layer with a learned policy.
No rule conflicts. The paper does not argue for dropping regular cosponsorship edges or for per-edge volume normalization, and it uses no LDA or reciprocity claims.
rel.paul_alignment: Paul's mapping is right in substance and is already built as SGATE. His mapping: a lobbied legislator may or may not take up an invitation, so contact is not activation. The receptivity docstring echoes it ('legislators know they are being lobbied'). The gate is applied inside the frontier and coalition spread estimators. Two parts of his note are stale or loose relative to the system and the paper. First, 'sequential, observe-then-act seeding' describes the paper's multi-round setting, but Melange seeds single-shot and never observes willingness, so that half of his takeaway is an extension, not current behaviour. Second, he files the paper in the non-submodular RL tier, but Chen 2021 assumes submodularity; the complex-contagion argument belongs to RL4CCIM. His broader expectation that a learned policy (GCOMB, RL) will replace greedy is not supported here. RL4IM only matches greedy, and its advantage is runtime on new graphs, which Melange does not face.

related.why: Same group (Chen, Tambe). It carries the RL-for-IM framing into complex contagion, which is the non-submodular regime that Paul's addendum attributes to this paper.

The paper contrasts itself with adaptive submodularity, which it says does not address uncertainty in node willingness. Golovin-Krause is the operational-layer bound the joint optimizer uses as a diagnostic.
Cited as RL for IM under graph-exploration uncertainty. It sits beside Chen as the other learned-policy entry in Paul's sequential-IM addendum.
SNAM behaviour-aware IM survey, cited together with Chen as 'Chen/SNAM' for seed_prob in receptivity_layer.py and outcome_contract.py H1.
Source of the competitive IC cascade into which the system inserts Chen's contingency gate. Chen models a single colour only.
Graph-embedding or GNN-based influence maximization: learned node representations for seed selection, as in RL4IM's structure2vec backbone.
Deep-RL influence maximization in the same S2V or DQN lineage, applied to edge activation instead of contingent seeds.
Questions whether greedy is needed at all. Read with Chen's parity-with-greedy result, it suggests learned or heuristic policies buy runtime, not quality, at Melange's scale.

paul_entries.text:
**Chen, H., Qiu, W., Ou, H.-C., An, B., & Tambe, M. (2021).** *Contingency-Aware Influence Maximization: A Reinforcement Learning Approach.* UAI '21 (PMLR). arXiv:2106.07039. https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.07039

RL for IM when chosen seeds may decline to participate — sequential, observe-then-act seeding under uncertainty about whether any given activation actually "takes." The contingency framing maps onto legislators who may or may not move when approached, and onto lobbying outreach where commitment is probabilistic rather than guaranteed.
